t.2.101.1: But having heard the words of Jābāli, Rāma, the foremost of those whose nature is truth, spoke with supreme reasoning and with his own unimpaired understanding.
t.2.101.2: The words you have spoken here out of a wish to please me describe what should not be done, though it looks like what should be done, and what is harmful, though it seems wholesome.
t.2.101.3: But a man who knows no bounds, given to sinful conduct, whose character is seen to be broken, gains no honour among the virtuous.
t.2.101.4: It is conduct alone that reveals whether a man is well-born or ill-born, a true hero or one who merely fancies himself a man, pure or impure.
t.2.101.5: But one who is ignoble yet seems noble, who is devoid of purity yet appears pure, who seems to bear auspicious marks yet lacks them, who is ill-natured yet seems virtuous in conduct,
t.2.101.7: What thoughtful man in this world, discerning between what should and should not be done, will hold me in high regard, a man of wicked conduct who brings disgrace upon the world?
t.2.101.6: If, abandoning what is good, I were to embrace this unrighteousness in the guise of righteousness, this confounding of the world, setting aside the rules of sacred rites…
t.2.101.9: This whole world, moreover, comes to behave according to its desires; for as kings conduct themselves, so do their subjects conduct themselves.
t.2.101.8: Whose conduct shall I follow, or by what means could I attain heaven, if I live by this way of life in which promises are abandoned?
t.2.101.10: Truth alone, together with compassion, is the eternal conduct of kings; therefore kingship has truth as its very essence, and on truth the world is founded.
t.2.101.11: The seers and the gods alike have held truth alone in honor, for in this world the speaker of truth attains the supreme abode.
t.2.101.12: Just as people recoil in fear from a snake, so they recoil from a man who speaks untruth. In this world truth is said to be the highest dharma and the root of heaven.
t.2.101.14: What is given in charity, what is offered in sacrifice, what is poured into the fire, and the austerities that are practised, and the Vedas too, all have truth as their foundation; therefore one should be wholly devoted to truth.
t.2.101.13: Truth alone is the lord in the world; it is truth in which Padmā takes her refuge. All things have truth as their root; there is no state higher than truth.
t.2.101.15: One alone protects the world, one alone protects the family; one alone sinks into hell, and one alone is honored in heaven.
t.2.101.16: Why then should I not carry out my father's command, I who am true to my promise and have bound myself to truth by truth itself?
t.2.101.17: Neither from greed nor from delusion, nor from ignorance, overcome by darkness, shall I break the bridge of truth, I who stand true to my father's promise.
t.2.101.18: From one who is false to his pledge, fickle and unsteady of mind, neither the gods nor the ancestors accept offerings. So we have heard.
t.2.101.20: I shall indeed abandon the warrior's dharma, which is adharma joined with dharma, practised by the base, the cruel and the greedy, men of sinful deeds.
t.2.101.19: I myself see this dharma, truth, as belonging to the inmost self. The burden that good men have borne is gladly welcomed for its sake.
t.2.101.21: Having first resolved upon it in the mind, one commits sin with the body, and with the tongue one speaks falsehood; thus sinful action is threefold.
t.2.101.22: Land, renown, glory and prosperity seek out the man who is truthful, and they follow him even when he dwells in heaven; therefore one should cleave to truth alone.
t.2.101.23: For what you, having considered my position, have told me with persuasive words, saying, 'Do this good thing,' may seem the best course, yet it would in truth be ignoble.
t.2.101.24: For how, having promised my father this dwelling in the forest, shall I carry out Bharata's word and abandon the word of my father?
t.2.101.25: In the presence of my elders I made a firm vow, and then Queen Kaikeyī became joyful at heart.
t.2.101.26: Thus dwelling in his forest exile, pure and restrained in his food, satisfying the ancestors and the gods with sacred roots, flowers and fruits.
t.2.101.27: With my five senses content, I carry on the business of the world, free of deceit and full of faith, discerning what ought and ought not to be done.
t.2.101.28: Having attained this land of action, one should perform deeds that are auspicious; for Agni, Vāyu and Soma are sharers in the fruits of deeds.
t.2.101.29: Having performed a hundred sacrifices, the king of the gods went to heaven; and by undertaking fierce austerities, the great seers went to heaven.
t.2.101.30: Truth and righteousness and valor, compassion for all beings and kindness of speech, and the worship of the twice-born, the gods and guests: these, the virtuous say, are the path to heaven.
t.2.101.31: Devoted to dharma, keeping company with good men, full of splendour, pre-eminent in the virtue of generosity, harmless and freed from impurity, such foremost sages become worthy of honour in the world.
